title: Divine Decree and Destiny: Taking Means, Then Tranquility of Heart
summary:
Your child returns from an exam or a game with a broken spirit, bitterly repeating: "If only I had done such-and-such, I would have succeeded! I always have bad luck!" Between the ages of ten and twelve, comparisons and frustrations escalate. This is where sound faith in divine decree and destiny becomes a great psychological fortress, protecting your child from two dangerous extremes: laziness under the pretext of "what is written," or self-blame and despair in the face of failure.

The Prophet ﷺ summarized this golden equation in the most eloquent way; he ﷺ said: "The strong believer is better and more beloved to Allah than the weak believer, and there is good in both" (Sahih Muslim 2664). And in the same hadith, he ﷺ said: "And if anything befalls you, do not say, 'If only I had done such-and-such, it would have been so-and-so,' but rather say, 'This is the decree of Allah, and He does what He wills'" (Sahih Muslim 2664). Reflect on this beautiful balance: before the outcome, we strive and take every means we can, seeking Allah's help. After the outcome occurs, we accept Allah's decree and destiny with a tranquil heart, then we rise to learn for the next time.

Do not teach your child this meaning when they are collapsing in a moment of loss; instead, embrace their disappointment first. Then, after they calm down, review two steps together: What means did we exert that we are proud of? And what can we improve in the next experience? When your child sees you content, tranquil, and submitting to Allah's command with a smile when your plans are disrupted or you miss something you love, they will learn true reliance on Allah through observation, not just words.
try_this: Tonight: Share with your child a situation that didn't go as you wished recently, and tell them how you took the necessary means then submitted your affair to Allah with contentment and calm. Agree that each of you will remind the other of this principle whenever there is a setback.
reflection_prompts: How does our home react to unexpected failure: with panic and repeating "if only," or with acceptance and correcting the course?
How do I clearly differentiate for my child between reliance on Allah (while taking means) and passive dependence and laziness?
parent_script: "You put in your effort, and I am proud of your striving; we accept what Allah has decreed for us with a tranquil heart, then we think together about what we can learn for next time."
assistant_prompts: My 11-year-old child collapses emotionally at the slightest loss or a single missed point. How can I raise them to be content and perseverant?
My child asks me: If everything is written, why do we strive and pray? How do I answer in a language they understand?
